newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: ICE SKATING-SPROUT FARMER WINS HEROIC DUTCH SKATING MARATHON.
newsitem.headline: ICE SKATING-SPROUT FARMER WINS HEROIC DUTCH SKATING MARATHON.

text.p: A 29-year-old sprout farmer won the legendary 200-kilometre (125-mile) Elfstedentocht (Eleven Cities Tour) skating marathon in the northern Netherlands on Saturday, completing the gruelling course in just under seven hours.
"This is the best day of my life," said Henk Angenent after sprinting home ahead of more than 16,000 others who took part in the marathon over the frozen canals of the Friesland province.

The Elfstedentocht, first held in 1909 and last staged 11 years ago, has taken on legendary status as it can only go ahead when temperatures drop low enough to provide at least 15 cms (six inches) of ice along the entire course which links 11 mediaeval Friesian towns.

The historic race began for only the 15th time this century, with the first group of 300 top marathon skaters being released from a steel cage in the Friesian capital of Leeuwarden at 5.30am (0430 GMT), emerging into darkness and the freezing cold.
Some wore miners' lamps attached to their headgear to help light their way.
Hours later, those in the "tourist" class were still setting off, hoping only to complete the race and have their own tales to tell of personal heroism and endurance.

Over a third of the field were aged over 50, including 1954 race winner Jeen van den Berg, 69, who was competing for the seventh time. The oldest skater was born in 1918 as the First World War drew to a close. The youngest was 18.
The last contestants, many carrying mobile phones to keep in touch with family and friends, were expected to complete the gruelling course by midnight.

Police said over half a million fans poured into the province, with tens of thousands partying deep into Friday night in Leeuwarden to celebrate an event which is both a major sporting occasion and a national festival.
Thousands more, wearing orange bobble-hats, lined the route, keeping warm to the constant beat of hundreds of oompah bands.
Millions watched live television coverage of the race, with the state electricity board noting a power surge in the early hours of Saturday as TV sets were switched on around the nation.
Angenent will become a folk hero but his material rewards will be modest compared with other top sporting stars.
Evert van Benthem, winner of the last two races in 1985 and 1986, continues to work as a dairy farmer even though his name is known the length and breadth of the Netherlands.
Hundreds of race marshalls, police and first aid attendants were on hand to ensure the smooth running of the event, while local hospitals dealt with dozens of skaters' broken bones.
Canny entrepreneurs cashed in on the carnival atmosphere, hawking Elfstedentocht T-shirts and souvenir paraphernalia.
